subtype: Approach: tracking actual screen time first [Action]
passage: Emre had guessed one hour. For a week in Ankara he opened the usage report on his phone each night and copied the numbers into a notebook: Monday, three hours ten. Tuesday, two hours fifty. By Sunday the total was over twenty hours, most of it short videos. He stared at the page. His friend Ulla leaned over and whistled. "Is that really yours?" "I thought it was one hour a day," Emre said quietly. Nobody had lectured him and no parent had counted. The numbers did it. That night he opened the settings, set a limit for the video app, and wrote in the margin: half of this. Not zero. Half.

qa.q: How much time had Emre guessed he spent on the phone?
What did Emre feel when he saw the total?
qa.a: Shocked and quiet, since he had thought it was one hour a day.

qa.q: What could Emre do beyond the limit on the video app?
qa.a: Fill some of that time with something planned, such as football or homework, because a limit works better with an alternative.

qa.q: How might Ulla see the notebook?
qa.a: With surprise, since Ulla whistled and asked whether the numbers were really Emre's.

grounding: A student checks the phone's usage report for a week, finds far more time on short videos than guessed, and the data makes him ready to change.

subtype: Approach: tracking actual screen time first [Action]
passage: In the Wednesday wellbeing period, Pallavi Ma'am didn't lecture. She just said, "Open your phone's screen-time report. Last seven days. Don't show anyone. Just look." Samir expected an hour, maybe an hour and a half. The number said 3 hours 12 minutes a day, almost all of it on the short-video app. He scrolled back day by day in case it was wrong. Tuesday: 3 hours 40. Sunday: 4 hours 5. He thought of the Maths homework he "hadn't had time for". Around him, others were going quiet too. "What you do with that is your business," Pallavi Ma'am said. Samir said nothing. But at lunch he moved the app off his home screen, into a folder three swipes deep, and set a daily limit of forty-five minutes.

qa.q: What was Samir's daily average on the report?
How did Samir feel when he saw the number?
qa.a: He felt shocked and uneasy; he had guessed about an hour and scrolled back day by day in case it was wrong.

qa.q: Why might the report work better than a lecture?
qa.a: Seeing his own numbers made the problem real and his own, so the change came from Samir rather than from being told.

qa.q: How might Pallavi Ma'am see the quiet classroom?
qa.a: She likely sees the data doing its job, and chooses not to push, leaving each student to decide.

grounding: Shows a student checking a week of phone usage data, finding three hours a day on short videos and becoming ready to change.

subtype: Approach: tracking actual screen time first [Action]
passage:
Hi Gopika Akka,
Remember at Diwali you said I was "always on my phone" and I said no I'm not? I checked. My phone keeps a usage report, so I looked at the whole last week. Short videos: 2 hours 58 minutes a day. Three hours. Every day. I honestly thought it was forty minutes. Sunday was over four. I added it up: that's more than twenty hours a week, more than all my tuition classes put together. Nobody had to tell me anything; the number did it. So I've set a one-hour limit on the app and moved it off the first screen. I'll check the report again next Sunday and send you the number, even if it's bad.
Your little brother,
Harsha

qa.q: How much time a day did Harsha spend on short videos?
How did Harsha feel seeing the report?
qa.a: Harsha was shocked and a bit embarrassed, having guessed only forty minutes.

qa.q: What could make Harsha's plan stick?
qa.a: Checking the report every Sunday as promised, so he can see whether the one-hour limit is working and adjust it.

qa.q: How might Gopika Akka feel reading the email?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and relieved that he saw it for himself, and touched that he'll share the number even if it's bad 🙂.

grounding: A student's email shows a week of usage data revealing three hours a day on short videos, and the numbers prompting change.
